flashcards.q: How is BigQuery on-demand pricing calculated and what's the free tier?
flashcards.a: $6.25 per TiB of logical bytes scanned (columns actually read), with the first 1 TiB per project per month free. Columnar storage means SELECT * scans every column's bytes -- no buffer cache saves you the way it does on a row-store warehouse.

flashcards.q: What are BigQuery Editions and their pay-as-you-go slot-hour rates?
flashcards.a: Standard $0.04, Enterprise $0.06, Enterprise Plus $0.10 per slot-hour (US region), replacing flat-rate slots retired 2023-07-05. Autoscaling slots (baseline + max, 100-slot increments) are the default capacity model, billed only while in use.

flashcards.q: Roughly where does the on-demand-vs-Editions break-even point sit?
flashcards.a: Around 400-500 TiB scanned per month. Below that, on-demand's pay-per-scan model wins; above it, a slot commitment typically amortizes cheaper -- but only if partitioning/clustering already control scan volume first.

flashcards.q: What is BigQuery's partition column restriction and hard partition-count limit?
flashcards.a: One DATE/TIMESTAMP/DATETIME/INTEGER column (or ingestion time). Hard cap: 4,000 partitions per table. Daily partitioning gives ~11 years of runway; hourly burns through the cap in ~5 months.

flashcards.q: How does BigQuery clustering differ from partitioning mechanically?
flashcards.a: Clusters on up to 4 columns, sorted in specified order (order matters -- sorts by col1 then col2 within that...), no limit on cardinality/partition count, works on more types. STRING clustering only uses the first 1,024 characters. Only helps when WHERE clauses filter on the clustered columns.

flashcards.q: What breaks incremental refresh on a JOIN-based BigQuery materialized view?
flashcards.a: Only the LEFT-side table of the JOIN can have appended data and stay incremental. Any change (append/update/delete) to a right-side table forces a full non-incremental rebuild. Default refresh attempt: within 5 min if prior refresh was >30 min stale; configurable cap 1 min to 7 days.

flashcards.q: Name the three layered BigQuery cost controls and what each catches.
flashcards.a: maximum_bytes_billed: per-query, pre-execution byte estimate, fails free if over threshold. Custom quotas: project/user daily scan cap (200 TiB default since 2025-09-01, resets midnight PT), approximate safeguard. Partitioning/clustering: fixes the root cause (bytes scanned) rather than capping after the fact. None alone is sufficient.

flashcards.q: What does Dataflow's Streaming Engine offload, and what does the autoscaling hint control?
flashcards.a: Offloads windowing, state, and timer management from worker VMs to a managed backend, making workers near-stateless so horizontal autoscaling (1 to 1000+ workers) is fast and responsive to backlog changes. Autoscaling hint 0.3 favors minimal latency, 0.7 favors minimal cost.

flashcards.q: What is Pub/Sub's default delivery guarantee, and how does exactly-once differ?
flashcards.a: Default: at-least-once -- redelivery possible even after ack, consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once delivery (GA) guarantees no redelivery once a message is successfully acked, at the cost of added ack latency -- reserved for cases where idempotent consumer design is impractical, not the default.

flashcards.q: How do Pub/Sub ordering keys work and what's the failure mode?
flashcards.a: Opt-in: messages with the same ordering key deliver in publish order; all messages for one key must publish to the same region (subscribers can be anywhere). Since delivery is still at-least-once underneath, one unacked/failed message blocks (head-of-line-blocks) all subsequent messages for that key until resolved -- mitigate with a dead-letter topic.

flashcards.q: Contrast Pub/Sub's and Kinesis's default ordering/exactly-once posture.
flashcards.a: Kinesis: ordering is free per-shard by construction, but exactly-once is never provided -- consumer must always dedupe. Pub/Sub: ordering is opt-in via ordering keys (with a same-region publish constraint), exactly-once is a GA managed opt-in feature. Opposite defaults.

Looker: enterprise semantic layer, LookML (modeling language compiled to governed SQL), no public pricing, real contracts land $60K-150K+/year, needs 1-2+ FTE to maintain. Looker Studio: free dashboard tool (Pro tier $9/user/month), no LookML, no governed semantic layer -- a lightweight reporting tool, not the enterprise product.
